Calcareous Egyptian soils are this species PREFERRED soil reaction, not merely tolerated. No vernalisation requirement is documented and TNAU classifies it as a winter crop in subtropical areas, matching an October to November transplant. Its native range already includes Morocco and Algeria. Binding constraint is salinity, not pH or heat: it is a glycophyte.

All parts are highly toxic (roots to 1.3 percent tropane alkaloids fresh weight). Cultivation is legal in Europe, North America, Pakistan and Brazil. NO Egypt-specific cultivation restriction was found, which is an open item to verify with the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Agriculture rather than an assurance. A field trial would need a fenced labelled plot, gloves at harvest, and no grazing access.

Tamil Nadu Agricultural University: nursery germination 3 weeks, transplant at 15-20 cm after 8-12 weeks, first herb cut about 3 months after transplanting at onset of flowering. Roots harvested in year 3. Yield 1000 kg/ha dry herb year 1, 1500 kg/ha years 2-3, total tropane alkaloids 0.13-0.70 percent.

No annual rainfall figure exists in any source checked. Substitute the measured irrigation criterion instead: irrigate back to field capacity at 35 percent depletion of available soil water, which maximises both root biomass and tropane alkaloid yield.

Grows wild across Egypt including Assiut, Middle Egypt, three Delta sites and three Mediterranean coast sites, with Delta populations giving the highest silymarin content. The binding constraint is thermal season, not pH: germination optimum is 2-15 C, so it must be autumn sown in October or November and harvested May to June. A spring or summer sowing will fail. Successfully trialled in an analogous hot arid irrigated setting at Al-Hassa, Saudi Arabia.

Plants completed a full cycle from rosette through bolting and flowering to viable seed on Greek field soils measured at pH 7.8 and 7.9.
